articles.title: New Simulations Connect the First Galaxies to the Universe We See Today
articles.description: In a recent study, researchers at the international MEGATRON project used some of the most detailed simulations of the early Universe to investigate how the first stars and galaxies formed.
articles.summary: The MEGATRON project's advanced simulations connect the formation of the first galaxies to the structure of the universe we observe today. This breakthrough provides crucial insights into cosmic evolution over billions of years.

articles.title: A gamma-ray burst's engine stayed active for nearly a month, breaking the previous record
articles.description: Astronomers have observed the longest-lasting central engine activity ever recorded from a gamma-ray burst. The burst occurred at a redshift of 0.8577, and the activity lasted about 27 days in the burst's own rest frame—around 20 days longer than the previous record. The paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 18, explores different mechanisms that could be powering this puzzling burst.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers have observed a record-breaking gamma-ray burst whose central engine remained active for nearly a month, shattering previous duration records and revealing new physics about these violent phenomena.

articles.title: Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
articles.description: Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid.
articles.summary: CERN physicists have captured the clearest evidence yet that quarks form waves in quark-gluon plasma, the primordial soup that existed immediately after the Big Bang.

articles.title: NASA’s Roman telescope just opened its planet-hunting eye
articles.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has demonstrated remarkable pointing stability and given its powerful planet-imaging coronagraph its first look at the cosmos. The telescope can already stay locked on a target with precision comparable to aiming a laser at a dime from about 150 miles away. Its coronagraph also captured stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, confirming that the instrument can produce focused images.
articles.summary: NASA's Roman Space Telescope has demonstrated exceptional pointing stability and unveiled its powerful planet-imaging coronagraph capabilities, marking a major milestone for exoplanet discovery.

articles.title: First Direct Image of Protoplanet Swirling Surrounding Gas
articles.description: The formation and evolution of planets is the driving force behind both where and how we might find life beyond Earth. This complex and lengthy process first begins with a massive ball of gas and dust that swirls until it flattens into a disk, followed by roc…
articles.summary: Astronomers have captured the first direct image of a protoplanet surrounded by swirling gas, advancing understanding of planetary formation. This discovery enhances knowledge of where and how life might exist beyond Earth.

articles.title: The Universe Is Full of Tiny Red Dots—and They’re One of Astronomy’s Biggest Discoveries in Decades
articles.description: A new type of object found in the early universe has puzzled astronomers for years, but they may finally have some answers.
articles.summary: Astronomers have identified a new class of mysterious red objects in the early universe, representing one of the biggest astronomical discoveries in decades. After years of puzzlement, researchers are gaining insights into these intriguing cosmic structures.

articles.title: SpaceX Just Proved Rocket Reuse Works Better Than Anyone Expected
articles.description: Putting things into outer space is expensive, that's why reusable rocket boosters have been the dream for decades, and SpaceX is making it work.
articles.summary: SpaceX has proven that reusable rocket boosters work better than expected, revolutionizing space launch economics. This breakthrough validates decades of engineering pursuit for affordable, sustainable spaceflight.

articles.title: From a remote Texas base, SpaceX's launch shows Louisiana what to expect. 'See the future.'
articles.description: SpaceX's Starship — a 40-story, two-stage behemoth, the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown — climbed over the Gulf as hundreds watched. Here’s what the scene was like in Texas as Musk’s Vermilion Parish spaceport begins to come to life.
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship, a 40-story two-stage mega-rocket, continues advancing as the most powerful rocket ever flown. The vehicle represents humanity's future capability for deep space exploration and beyond.

articles.title: NASA's First Selection for a New Class of Mission: The PRIMA Far-Infrared Telescope
articles.description: NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space telescope is the first in a new class of NASA astrophysics …
articles.summary: NASA selected PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission) to explore the history and evolution of the universe using far-infrared observations. This landmark mission will unveil previously hidden cosmic phenomena.

articles.title: Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.description:
Image:
			Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope captures detailed imagery of stellar jets erupting from a nebula, revealing dynamic cosmic phenomena. This observation showcases Webb's ability to study star formation and the energetic processes within stellar nurseries.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The Smile mission, a joint European-Chinese effort, has begun its science operations studying Earth's interaction with solar wind. This landmark mission will provide unprecedented insights into magnetospheric dynamics and space weather.

articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals intricate details of distant galaxies through gravitational lensing effects. This Picture of the Month demonstrates Webb's extraordinary capability to study galaxy structure and formation.

articles.title: Successful Earth flyby improves Juice’s course to Jupiter
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) skimmed the very outer edge of Earth’s atmosphere on 28 September, using the gravity of our home planet to alter its route to Jupiter using very little fuel.
articles.summary: ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) successfully completed a gravity assist maneuver around Earth, refining its trajectory toward Jupiter. This pivotal flyby brings the mission closer to exploring the Jovian system's icy moons.

articles.title: A Buried Volcano on the Moon Hints At An Ancient Lunar Dynamo
articles.description: Scientists know for certain the moon doesn’t currently have a magnetosphere. But they’ve been debating for decades about whether it ever did. Data from both Apollo samples and orbital scientific instruments have proven divisive, and so the debate still rages. But a new paper from researchers at ETH Zurich, DLR, and the Institute of Applied Geosciences hopes to resolve the debate once and for all - by definitively proving that the Moon did, indeed, once have a magnetic dynamo.
articles.summary: Scientists discover evidence of a buried lunar volcano that hints at an ancient magnetic field protecting the Moon's surface. This finding revolutionizes our understanding of the Moon's early geological and magnetic history.

articles.title: Chandra X-ray Observatory Drops New View of our Galaxy’s Unruly Centre
articles.description: The core of the Milky Way is a dense, active, messy region, dominated by a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) hiding at the heart of the galaxy. But Sgr A* is only a supporting actor in this stunning new image from the Chandra X-ray Observatory.
articles.summary: The Chandra X-ray Observatory reveals new details about Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. These observations illuminate the dynamic and energetic processes occurring at the galactic core.

articles.title: Neutrons, Rotating Black Holes, and a Galactic PeVatron at the Center of the Milky Way
articles.description: Supermassive black holes generate tremendous amounts of energy through their accretion disks and jets. But they can also generate energy through the magnetic Penrose process. A new study looks at how we might observe this process through multimessenger astronomy.
articles.summary: Research reveals how supermassive black holes generate extreme energy and particle acceleration, creating galactic PeVatrons at the Milky Way's center. This study enhances our understanding of the universe's most powerful cosmic engines.

articles.title: XRISM Makes First-Ever Detection of a Pulsar Feeding from a Companion's Stellar "Wind"
articles.description: Using data from the Japan-led XRISM observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star’s stellar wind captured by its compact companion (triggering X-ray flares) for the first time.
articles.summary: Japan's XRISM observatory has made the first direct observation of a pulsar feeding on stellar wind from a companion star, advancing our understanding of these exotic cosmic systems.

articles.title: Webb captures commotion from nebula's stellar jets
articles.description: The NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope has unveiled numerous stars formerly hidden by clouds of dust in a stellar nursery known as NGC 7129—a cauldron of cosmic creation, 3,300 light-years from Earth. Webb captured infrared light, which pierces through the dense matter that scatters or absorbs other types of light. This region, rife with stellar objects in different stages of their lives, offers an opportunity to explore how stars shape their surroundings.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed previously hidden stars within a stellar nursery by penetrating dust clouds and capturing the dynamic jets of stellar formation in unprecedented detail.

articles.title: Striking new images of unique supernova remnant reveal pearl-like chains
articles.description: The only known supernova remnant of its kind in the Milky Way has an unexpectedly intricate structure: chains of gas knots resembling pearls on a string, each wide enough to fit the solar system multiple times. Using the Gemini North telescope, an international team co-led by Ilaria Caiazzo, assistant professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), captured the most detailed view yet of Pa 30, revealing striking new features of the remnant associated with a historical supernova witnessed nearly 850 years ago. The findings are published in The Astrophysical Journal.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Striking new observations reveal the Milky Way's only known supernova remnant of its unique type features an unexpectedly intricate structure of pearl-like gas chains.

articles.title: Where are the best places for life in the cosmos? A universe in a supercomputer yields an answer
articles.description: Earth seems like a troubled place right now, but at least our cosmic surroundings appear peaceful. This is not universally true, as explosions, collisions and other dangers lurk in other places and times.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Supercomputer simulations of the universe identify the most favorable cosmic locations for life to flourish, expanding our perspective on habitability across the cosmos.

articles.title: This mysterious hole on the Moon may open into a giant cave
articles.description: NASA has selected the GIMLI project to investigate whether the Marius Hill Pit opens into a vast underground cave or lava tube. Using radar, seismic sensors, gravity measurements, and cameras, researchers will search beneath the lunar surface and estimate the size of any hidden void. Such caves could preserve clues to the Moon’s volcanic history and potentially provide protected shelters for future astronauts.
articles.summary: NASA has selected the GIMLI project to investigate whether the Marius Hill Pit on the Moon opens into a vast underground cave, potentially revealing lunar geology and habitability.

articles.title: Scientists find a surprising clue to why the universe’s expansion doesn’t add up
articles.description: Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Detailed simulations show that these primordial fields could have changed the formation of hydrogen in the early universe, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.
articles.summary: New research suggests that tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help resolve the long-standing disagreement about the universe's expansion rate.

articles.title: ESA’s Juice just used Earth as a slingshot to Jupiter
articles.description: ESA’s Juice spacecraft raced past Earth on September 28, using our planet’s gravity to dramatically reshape its path toward Jupiter without burning much fuel. The flyby changed its direction by 20 degrees and increased its speed by 3.5 km/s, while also giving scientists a rare chance to test its instruments on Earth and the Moon.
articles.summary: ESA's Juice spacecraft successfully performed a gravitational slingshot maneuver around Earth on September 28, reshaping its trajectory toward Jupiter for its groundbreaking mission.

articles.title: Chang’e-6 lunar soil contains a surprising magnetic time capsule
articles.description: Scientists studying Chang’e-6 lunar soil have discovered a previously unknown magnetic mineral in natural Moon samples: a form of metallic iron called γ-Fe. Found inside tiny impact-glass particles, the nanoscale iron can preserve a stable magnetic signal, potentially acting like a microscopic fossil of the Moon’s long-lost magnetic field.
articles.summary: Analysis of Chang'e-6 lunar samples has revealed a previously unknown magnetic mineral, providing a time capsule of the Moon's ancient magnetic history and geological evolution.

articles.title: STARMUS FESTIVAL COFOUNDERS SIR BRIAN MAY AND GARIK ISRAELIAN PRESENTED PROFESSOR BRIAN COX WITH THE 2026 STEPHEN HAWKING MEDAL FOR SCIENCE COMMUNICATION
articles.description: LONDON, Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On October 2nd, At the Royal Astronomical Society in London, Starmus Festival cofounders Sir Brian May and Garik Israelian awarded Professor Brian Cox the prestigious 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication, r…
articles.summary: Professor Brian Cox received the 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication at the Royal Astronomical Society, presented by Starmus Festival cofounders Sir Brian May and Garik Israelian. The award honors outstanding contributions to communicating space science to the public.

articles.title: SpaceX a envoyé quatre astronautes à bord de l’ISS en moins de 8 heures : le trajet le plus rapide jamais réalisé par un équipage américain
articles.description: Sept heures et cinquante-cinq minutes. C'est le temps qu'il a fallu à quatre astronautes pour rallier l'ISS à bord d'un Crew Dragon, battant largement le précédent record américain, et enterrant au passage l'une des plus tenaces superstitions de la NASA.
articles.summary: SpaceX transported four astronauts to the International Space Station in 7 hours and 55 minutes, achieving the fastest crewed journey to the ISS in American spaceflight history. This milestone demonstrates SpaceX's advancing capabilities for rapid human spaceflight operations.

articles.title: Η NASA ψάχνει για κρυφό γιγάντιο σπήλαιο κάτω από τη Σελήνη – Η «τρύπα» που μπορεί να κρύβει έναν τεράστιο υπόγειο κόσμο
articles.description: Ραντάρ, σεισμικοί αισθητήρες, βαρυόμετρο και κάμερες θα αναζητήσουν κάτω από την επιφάνεια της Σελήνης στοιχεία για έναν πιθανό τεράστιο υπόγειο σχηματισμό
articles.summary: NASA is searching for hidden giant caves beneath the lunar surface using radar, seismic sensors, and advanced imaging technology. Discovery of subsurface voids could reveal a vast underground environment and support future lunar exploration and habitation.

articles.title: Le jet supersonique silencieux X-59 n’avait jamais volé aussi vite ni aussi souvent
articles.description: Le X-59, l'avion supersonique « silencieux » de la NASA, a atteint Mach 1,53 lors d'un vol d'essai fin septembre 2026. Il n'avait jamais volé aussi vite, et il a aussi enchaîné six vols en une seule semaine, un autre record pour l'appareil.
articles.summary: NASA's X-59 experimental aircraft achieved Mach 1.53 in late September 2026, demonstrating advances in supersonic flight technology. This milestone represents progress toward quiet supersonic travel.

articles.title: SpaceX's Starship Needs To Be Fully Operational By 2028 — Here's Why
articles.description: SpaceX has plenty left to test on Starship, from refueling to docking in orbit, and NASA is counting on it to finish in time for a much bigger assignment.
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship is progressing through critical testing phases and must achieve full operational status by 2028 for NASA's lunar missions. The vehicle continues advancing through orbital refueling and docking demonstrations.

articles.title: Is SpaceX's Starship The Most Powerful Rocket Ever Built?
articles.description: SpaceX fitted Starship's first-stage booster with 33 engines, enough to make you wonder how it compares with the most powerful rockets humans have ever built.
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship features 33 first-stage engines, positioning it among the most powerful rockets ever constructed. This engineering achievement enables ambitious missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
